packages.name: Farming & herding
packages.description: A changing bundle of crops, animals and practical knowledge. Components arrived at different times; these regional milestones do not imply one uniform Neolithic package worldwide.

packages.name: Ironworking
packages.description: Turning ore into iron and forging iron into objects are different operations. A worked iron object alone is not proof that iron was smelted locally.

packages.name: Algebra
packages.description: A mathematical tradition with many antecedents and later developments. These records follow one influential Arabic treatise and a Latin translation; they do not locate the invention of all algebra.

packages.name: Movable-type printing
packages.description: Related techniques appeared in different settings. Korean and European milestones are recorded separately; this dataset does not claim a demonstrated transmission between them.

packages.name: Writing & record keeping
packages.description: Different writing traditions developed in different settings. These records attest specific scripts and uses, not a single invention spreading everywhere.

packages.name: Paper & papermaking
packages.description: A surviving paper object establishes use, not necessarily local manufacture. Traditional accounts of innovation are distinguished from archaeological firsts.

attestations.name: Cereal cultivation · Middle East
attestations.summary: The museum dates cereal cultivation here to approximately 9000 BCE. Livestock domestication followed over later millennia.
attestations.location_note: Representative regional point, not an excavated site or an origin coordinate.

attestations.name: Livestock domestication · Middle East
attestations.summary: The cited overview places the domestication of these animals in this interval. It does not imply simultaneous domestication at one location.
attestations.location_note: Representative regional point. Individual species and domestication centres need finer records.

attestations.name: Farming societies · Mediterranean
attestations.summary: Farming communities spread around the Mediterranean during this broad interval.
attestations.location_note: Schematic regional anchor; not a coastline-wide adoption boundary.

attestations.name: Farmers north of the Alps
attestations.summary: The overview places farming communities across much of central Europe by about this date.
attestations.location_note: Representative regional point, not a precise frontier.

attestations.name: Farming reaches Britain
attestations.summary: Farming appears in Britain around 4000 BCE; ancient-DNA research supports arrival with migrant farmers from continental Europe.
attestations.location_note: Representative point for Britain, not the first farm or a claim about every locality.

attestations.name: Iron smelting at Tell Hammeh
attestations.summary: Excavated production debris documents ore-to-metal ironmaking. This is an attested operation, not a claim to the earliest invention of smelting.
attestations.location_note: Approximate site vicinity; not a survey coordinate.

attestations.name: Iron smithing at Beth-Shemesh
attestations.summary: Excavations identified a large smithing operation. Forging iron is recorded separately from smelting ore.
attestations.location_note: Approximate site vicinity. No transfer route from Tell Hammeh is inferred.

attestations.name: Al-Khwarizmi’s algebra treatise
attestations.summary: Al-Khwarizmi set out systematic equation-solving in Arabic. Dates around 820 and 830 both occur in the literature; the display retains that uncertainty.
attestations.location_note: City-level anchor for the scholarly setting, not the location of a surviving manuscript.

attestations.name: Robert of Chester’s Latin translation
attestations.summary: Robert of Chester translated al-Khwarizmi’s algebra into Latin here. This is textual transmission, not proof that the subject was immediately taught across Europe.
attestations.location_note: City-level anchor. The connecting line is not a reconstructed manuscript journey.

attestations.name: Jikji printed with metal type
attestations.summary: The surviving Jikji volume records movable-metal-type printing at Heungdeok-sa. It is evidence of Korean printing, not of a known route to Gutenberg.
attestations.location_note: City-level anchor for the historical printing site.

attestations.name: Gutenberg Bible
attestations.summary: Gutenberg and Fust produced the Bible at Mainz. This European milestone does not erase earlier East Asian printing traditions.
attestations.location_note: City-level anchor; no Korea-to-Mainz transfer is asserted.

attestations.name: Caxton printing in Bruges
attestations.summary: Caxton printed in Bruges before establishing his Westminster press.
attestations.location_note: City-level anchor, not a workshop footprint.

attestations.name: Caxton’s Westminster press
attestations.summary: Caxton moved his press from Bruges to Westminster around this date.
attestations.location_note: Approximate Westminster anchor. The line illustrates a documented move, not its travel itinerary.

attestations.name: Mound cultivation at Kuk Swamp
attestations.summary: Excavated features support agricultural development in New Guinea. This record uses the cited calibrated interval, rather than treating all earlier plant exploitation as proven farming.
attestations.location_note: Approximate site vicinity, not a plot boundary.

attestations.name: Maize and squash in the Balsas region
attestations.summary: Microfossils and dated archaeological context support early cultivation in Mexico. This is a regional evidence interval, not a claim that maize was already a staple everywhere.
attestations.location_note: Illustrative Balsas regional anchor; not an exact excavation coordinate.

attestations.name: Proto-cuneiform at Uruk
attestations.summary: Early tablets document record keeping and developing sign systems. They do not establish that all writing originated at one known place or moment.
attestations.location_note: Approximate ancient-city anchor, not a tablet findspot.

attestations.name: Shang oracle-bone inscriptions
attestations.summary: Oracle-bone inscriptions preserve a selective record of Shang elite concerns. They are not evidence of universal literacy or a transfer from Mesopotamia.
attestations.location_note: Regional anchor for the Shang inscription tradition, not an individual object findspot.

attestations.name: Iron objects at Llyn Fawr
attestations.summary: The deposited assemblage attests access to worked iron. Neither local ore smelting nor a particular transmission route follows from the findspot.
attestations.location_note: Approximate lake vicinity; manufacture place is not established.

attestations.name: Iron chariot tyre at Llyn Cerrig Bach
attestations.summary: An iron chariot component attests skilled working of iron. Its deposition in Wales does not establish where the ore was smelted.
attestations.location_note: Approximate lake/find area, not the current museum location.

attestations.name: Early iron production at Meroe
attestations.summary: Excavation and dating identify an early production phase. Later changes in the location of ironmaking complicate any claim of uninterrupted activity at the same workshops.
attestations.location_note: Approximate city vicinity; not a surveyed furnace location.

attestations.name: Brahmagupta’s mathematical treatise
components: arithmetic with zero and negative quantities
attestations.summary: The Brahmasphutasiddhanta includes arithmetic and algebraic methods. The mapped place is where the author says he wrote it, rather than his sometimes-assumed birthplace.
attestations.location_note: City-level writing-place anchor, not a manuscript findspot.

attestations.name: Cai Lun’s papermaking report
attestations.evidence: historical account of a reported process
attestations.summary: The traditional account dates a report to the imperial court to 105 CE. This is not treated as the first archaeological occurrence or sole invention of paper.
attestations.location_note: Illustrative Han court-region anchor, not a securely located workshop.

attestations.name: Paper cut-out made in Egypt
attestations.summary: The museum dates this paper object to the tenth century and attributes its manufacture to Egypt. It does not establish the location of a paper mill or an exact adoption date.
attestations.location_note: Illustrative Egyptian regional anchor, not the object's documented findspot.

transmissions.summary: A Latin translation of the Arabic treatise is documented. The line connects intellectual endpoints, not a known direct journey from Baghdad to Segovia.
Caxton moved his printing press from Bruges to Westminster. The line is schematic.
